Filthiness
fĭlth´i-ness
n. (moral and ceremonial pollution; rendering Hebrew niddah, tumah, Greek molusmos, rhuparia)
From Anglo-Saxon fylth, from ful, foul. Scripture's use is deliberately physical: sin is spoken of as dirt because dirt must be washed, not excused.

Biblical Definition

Filthiness is Scripture's tactile word for pollution, and its force lies in the fact that filth cannot be reasoned with — it can only be cleansed. Hezekiah's reformation begins with the command to “carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place” (2Ch 29:5), which is what every genuine revival does first. Proverbs names the fatal self-assessment: “There is a generation that are pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed from their filthiness” (Pro 30:12) — sincerity about oneself is no cleansing agent. Isaiah's picture of the drunken feast is unsparing: “all tables are full of vomit and filthiness, so that there is no place clean” (Isa 28:8). And Ezekiel promises what no reformation of behaviour achieves — “I… will consume thy filthiness out of thee” (Eze 22:15). Paul then turns it all into a command grounded in promise: “let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (2Co 7:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines filthiness as foulness, dirtiness, and then as corruption, pollution, defilement by sin — and as that which pollutes, whatever the eye or the heart is defiled by.

FILTH´INESS, n. The state of being filthy.

2. Foulness; dirtiness; filth; nastiness.

3. Corruption; pollution; defilement by sin; impurity.

Let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit. 2 Cor. vii.

Key Scripture

2Co 7:1 — "Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God."

Pro 30:12 — "There is a generation that are pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed from their filthiness."

2Ch 29:5 — "And said unto them, Hear me, ye Levites, sanctify now yourselves, and sanctify the house of the LORD God of your fathers, and carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place."

Eze 22:15 — "And I will scatter thee among the heathen, and disperse thee in the countries, and will consume thy filthiness out of thee."

Modern Corruption

Defilement dismissed as an outdated category — nothing can pollute a person, only harm them — so that purity is left with no meaning and cleansing with nothing to do.

expand to see more

The modern moral vocabulary has one axis: harm. What injures no one cannot be wrong, and so the whole biblical category of defilement is unintelligible — a man may fill his eyes and mind with anything at all provided no victim can be produced. Scripture's answer is that the man himself is the victim, and that the temple in question is his own body. Filth is real whether or not it is actionable, and this is precisely why the gospel offers washing rather than merely acquittal.

Proverbs 30:12 is the verse for a self-assured age: pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed. Self-assessment cannot cleanse, because the eyes doing the assessing are part of what needs washing. Hezekiah's pattern is the alternative — the filthiness is carried out of the holy place first, and worship follows — and 2 Corinthians 7:1 orders it rightly for the believer: having therefore these promises, cleanse yourselves. The promises come first; the scrubbing is a response, never a payment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew niddah (H5079), impurity, that which is put away; tumah (H2932), ceremonial uncleanness; Greek molusmos (G3436), defilement — Paul's word in 2Co 7:1.

expand to see more

Hebrew niddah (H5079) — impurity, separation; used of ceremonial uncleanness and of Jerusalem's filthiness in her skirts (Lam 1:9).

Hebrew tumah (H2932) — uncleanness, defilement; what Ezekiel promises to consume out of the people (Eze 22:15).

Greek molusmos (G3436) — a staining, defilement; of flesh and spirit alike, so the inward is not exempt (2Co 7:1).

Usage

"“Carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place” — where reformation always begins."

"“Pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed” — sincerity is not a cleansing agent."

"“Let us cleanse ourselves… perfecting holiness in the fear of God” — response, not payment."
